premise: The Rejue Chaka section (33°37′08″N; 86° 51′23″E) is situated in the middle part of the Qiangtang Basin (Fig. 1b), where the PermianTriassic succession comprises the Rejue Chaka Formation below and Kanglu Formation above (Fig. 2).
The ~125-m-thick Rejue Chaka Formation was deposited in deltaic environments.
The lower part of the Rejue Chaka Formation consists largely of shale intercalated with limestone.
Abundant fusulinids were observed, including Gallowayinella meitienensis, G. qiangtangensis, Reichelina gujoiensis, R. pulchra, Dunbarula nana, and Codonofusiella sp. (Li et al., 2010).

Li et al. (2010) thus established Gallowayinella Zone (Fig. 3), which is typically near the Wuchiapingian/Changhsingian boundary.
The middle part of the Rejue Chaka Formation, consisting of finegrained sandstone, medium-grained sandstone, intercalated with limestone, displays an overall coarsening-upward sequence (Fig. 3).

Abundant fusulinids were observed, including Palaeofusulina sinensis Sheng, P. ninima, P. wangi Sheng, Reichelina changhsingensis Sheng et Chen, Reichelina pulchra R. M-Macley, and Reichelina gaqoiensis Wang (Li et al., 2010).
The Changhsingian fusulinid fauna is characterized by a dominance of Palaeofusulina (Wang et al., 2006).
The WuchiapingianChanghsingian boundary in South China was previously defined by the appearance of Changhsingian fusulinid Palaeofusulina (Rui and Sheng, 1981).
Reichelina changhsingensis Sheng et Chen and R. pulchra R. MMacley are both characteristic forms of the Changhsingian fusulinid fauna in South China (Wang et al., 2006).

Li et al. (2010) thus established Palaeofusulina-Reichelina Zone in the Qiangtang Basin (Fig. 3), corresponding to the Early Changhsingian Stage (Wang et al., 2006).
The upper part of the Rejue Chaka Formation consists mainly of coal-bearing mudstone.

Abundant plant fossils were observed in the coal-bearing mudstone bed, including Gigantonoclea meridionalis, Lobatannularia ensiforia, Sphenophyllum speciosum (Royle) McCl, Gigantopteris sp., Rajahia (Pecopteris) calcerformis, Pecopteris shuanghuensis, Cladophlebis cf. permica Lee and Wang, Pecopteris sp., Alethopteris sinensis, and Annularia pingleensis (Li et al., 2010).
These species are common in the Qiangtang Basin.
They occur above Palaeofusulina sinensis (Yao, 1978).

Yao (1978) proposed that the age of the Gigantopteris Coal Series in different places of South China is not exactly the same and ranges from the late Early Permian to the close of the epoch, while several elements of the Gigantopteris-Flora, such as Gigantopteris, Pecopteris, Annularia, and Lobatannularia may survive to the Early Triassic as relics.

Here, we place these species in the MiddleLate Changhsingian Stage based on the stratigraphic sequence and contact relationship.
Ash-bearing mudstones occur at the top of the Rejue Chaka Formation.
No fossil was found in these ash-bearing mudstones.
The PTB cannot be accurately defined on the base of fusulinids, because the fusulinids have completely disappeared worldwide below this level.
Particularly, in the Meishan section, the latest forms were found one meter below the Bed 27 (Zhao et al., 1981).
Thus, dating precision of the PTB is difficult in the Qiangtang Basin.

However, the ash-bearing mudstone bed may represent the Permian-Triassic transition based on fusulinids and sea-level changes (the lowermost sea level, see Section 5.1).
The Kanglu Formation contains largely red fine sandstones and conglomerates (in places), limestone, and siltstone with the characteristic Triassic bivalve Claraia.

Yao (1978) proposed that the age of the Gigantopteris Coal Series in different places of South China is not exactly the same and ranges from the late Early Permian to the close of the epoch, while several elements of the Gigantopteris-Flora, such as Gigantopteris, Pecopteris, Annularia, and Lobatannularia may survive to the Early Triassic as relics.

Here, we place these species in the MiddleLate Changhsingian Stage based on the stratigraphic sequence and contact relationship.
Ash-bearing mudstones occur at the top of the Rejue Chaka Formation.
No fossil was found in these ash-bearing mudstones.
The PTB cannot be accurately defined on the base of fusulinids, because the fusulinids have completely disappeared worldwide below this level.
Particularly, in the Meishan section, the latest forms were found one meter below the Bed 27 (Zhao et al., 1981).
Thus, dating precision of the PTB is difficult in the Qiangtang Basin.

However, the ash-bearing mudstone bed may represent the Permian-Triassic transition based on fusulinids and sea-level changes (the lowermost sea level, see Section 5.1).
